evidences.title: Refugee crisis and terrorism dominate downbeat Davos | Larry Elliott in Davos | The Guardian
evidences.content:
This years meeting was concerned with the plight of Europes refugees, the rise of Isis, the consequences of Brexit, and financial market turmoil

For Justin Welby, mulling over the state of the world in Davos has been easier than the previous week spent trying to hammer out an Anglican church compromise over gay marriage. The Archbishop of Canterbury even cracked one of the better jokes at the World Economic Forum.

Asked whether god is in cyberspace, Welby replied: I think he must be because every time I am on the underground or a bus I see people looking at their computer or mobile phone saying oh god, why wont this work.

Humour has been in short supply at this years Davos. The optimism of a year ago that the global economy was on the up after the deep slump of 2008-09 has disappeared fast. Five big fears have dominated the meeting.

The first has been the refugee crisis, now seen not just as a humanitarian tragedy but as a threat to the continued existence of the European Union. Mark Rutte, the Dutch prime minister, set the tone when he said a solution had to be found before better weather in the spring leads to a surge in the number of people seeking asylum from the civil war in Syria.

Justine Greening, the UK development secretary, Gordon Brown, the former prime minister, and Jim Kim, the president of the World Bank, all made the case for investment in building up the resilience of countries in the Middle East so that there will be less incentive for refugees to leave. For months, the World Bank has been working on a plan for how to deal with what it considers to be its number one issue.

Any long-term reconstruction plan, while necessary, is going to come too late to stop refugees making the dangerous journey to Europe in 2016. As David Miliband, the former foreign secretary and now president of the International Rescue Committee, said: We have got to get real about this. If any of us lived in Syria we would be trying to get to Europe. The higher you build the wall, the more you empower the people smugglers.

Some European nations have started to lay the first bricks in that wall, raising the fear not just of an uncoordinated response but of the dismantling of free movement, one of the pillars of the EU. If the existential threat to Europe last year was Greeces exit from the eurozone, this years threat is the collapse of the passport-free zone created by the Schengen agreement. European leaders are far more worried about that than they were about the return of the drachma in Greece.

Europes state of near-panic about refugees meant it was unable to focus fully on a third Davos issue  whether Britain would decide to leave the European Union. David Cameron would dearly like to conclude his renegotiation talks next month so that a referendum could be called in June, but he appeared to recognise that might not be possible. If there is a good deal on the table I will take it. But if there isnt the right deal I am not in a hurry. I can hold my referendum any time up until the end of 2017. With polls suggesting a tight contest, Brexit was being taken seriously.

The state of the financial markets provided the fourth reason for nervousness. Davos opened with shares in freefall amid concerns that Chinas economic slowdown was in fact a full-scale recession which would engulf the rest of the world economy. Mario Draghi prompted a rally by the end of the week, but the fact that the president of the European Central Bank could have such an impact with an unspecified pledge highlighted the manic depressive state of the markets.

Finally, the activities of Islamic State (Isis) in Iraq and Syria, and the terrorist attacks on Paris, have led to a heightened awareness of security risks. Even the breakthroughs in financial technology  hailed by some as the advent of a fourth industrial revolution  were seen as an opportunity for attacks by cyberterrorists.

Not everyone was consumed with gloom at Davos. Despite the geopolitical trauma of the last 12 months, John Kerry told delegates that they were not the victims of a pre-destined future.

The US secretary of state said: People dont fly to Davos to celebrate the status quo. Youve come here to change the world for the better, and define the future.

Kerrys optimism, though, was untypical. The theme of Davos 2016 was that the immediate future will be similar to the recent past: full of problems.
